_doc: Pinned claims: properties that are load-bearing and invisible to ordinary tests.
RULES, learned the hard way and not negotiable:
1. Pin by SIGNATURE, not by literal. Assert the smallest fragment that carries
the meaning, so a legitimate rewrite passes and a deletion fails. Pin a whole
sentence and every honest edit goes red, you get tired of it, and you start
editing the guard instead of the code. A guard people learn to edit is worse
than no guard, because it still looks like one.
2. Comments are stripped before searching. Otherwise a deleted sentence, quoted
in the comment explaining its deletion, satisfies the test protecting it.
3. Search the WHOLE app, never one file. A port legitimately moves copy into a
shared component. A guard that only looks at the original page reports every
relocation as a loss and is noise within a day.
4. A pin must be green the moment it is written. A pin that is red before the
work starts is a bad pin: fixing it afterwards is indistinguishable from
covering up a deletion, including to yourself.
active:false means the property does not exist yet and the pin is a SPEC, not a
guard. The gate reports pending pins separately and never counts them as passing.
Flip to active:true in the same commit that writes the property.

pins.why: The entire point of owning the domain - he built the first site in 2023 because he disliked an email domain that went nowhere. He has two addresses in circulation and named this one canonical; the old accounts@ address must never reappear.
A portfolio that does not say whose it is, in text a crawler can read, has failed at its only job.

These projects are AI-assisted and the site says so. This is the first line a later polish pass deletes, because it reads as self-deprecating ornament rather than the thing that makes every other claim believable. It is the single most load-bearing sentence on the site.

Every project claim names its own limit in the same breath as the claim. A recruiter who finds one overstatement discounts the entire page, so the caveats are what make the rest believable. Enforced structurally in ops/sanity.mjs (every project must carry a limit field); this pin holds the phrases that must never all vanish at once.
Keyboard and screen-reader users hit the nav on every page without one. Invisible to sighted testing, so nothing else will ever catch its removal.

The AI question sits in the ordinary run of questions on /answers/, not first and not last. Proportion IS the honesty mechanism the panel chose: elevated it becomes a confession, buried it becomes an evasion, and either reads worse than the plain answer. A later editor will want to move it for entirely reasonable-sounding reasons. This pin and the browser check that pairs with it are the only things that would notice.
